paragraphs: A linear bandit algorithm repeatedly chooses actions while learning from limited feedback about their outcomes. This paper asks how one algorithm can perform well both when outcomes follow a stable statistical pattern and when the environment behaves adversarially. These settings place different demands on exploration, so the goal is a method with strong guarantees in both.

The authors construct an algorithm using exploration by optimization. Their analysis gives an adversarial regret bound of O(d sqrt(T log T)) and a stochastic bound of O(d² log T / Δ_min). Here, regret measures the accumulated performance shortfall, d is the action set's dimension, T is the number of rounds, and Δ_min is the smallest gap separating an inferior action from the best one.

The bounds show nearly optimal performance across the two environments: the stochastic guarantee grows logarithmically with time, while the adversarial guarantee accommodates a harder setting. The paper also derives stronger guarantees for special cases, including ordinary multi-armed bandits and multitask bandits.
neurips-2023-an-exploration-by-optimizat.tldr: Exploration by optimization yields a linear bandit algorithm with nearly optimal regret guarantees in both stochastic and adversarial environments.

paragraphs: Object detectors need confidence estimates that meaningfully reflect how reliable their predictions are. A detector can locate and classify objects well while still being overly confident about mistakes. This paper addresses that problem for detection transformers, extending calibration work beyond the classification setting that has received most of the attention.

Cal-DETR changes training through two complementary mechanisms. First, it estimates uncertainty in a transformer detector and uses that uncertainty to adjust class logits, the scores underlying class predictions. Second, it mixes logits as a form of regularization alongside detection-specific losses. Together, these mechanisms aim to improve confidence estimates while preserving the detector's ability to recognize and locate objects.

The approach is developed for Deformable-DETR, UP-DETR, and DINO. Experiments cover three in-domain and four out-of-domain scenarios. Against competing methods that also calibrate during training, the reported results improve calibration in both settings while maintaining or sometimes improving detection performance. The findings support treating confidence quality as a training objective alongside detection quality.
neurips-2023-cal-detr-calibrated-detecti.tldr: Cal-DETR uses uncertainty-guided score adjustment and logit mixing during training to improve detection-transformer calibration while preserving detection performance.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary 3D detection asks a system to find objects in a scene using a flexible list of category names. With annotations available for only limited base categories, the system faces two connected problems: locating unfamiliar objects and assigning categories to their boxes. CoDA tackles both within one jointly learned framework.

For localization, the method combines prior knowledge about 3D box geometry with open-vocabulary semantic information from 2D imagery. This produces provisional box labels for novel objects. A second component aligns point-cloud features with image and text features. Its alignment includes both category-independent and category-discriminating components, using annotated base objects together with progressively discovered novel objects.

The components reinforce each other: newly discovered boxes supply material for alignment, and improved alignment helps localization. Experiments on SUN-RGBD and ScanNet support the effectiveness of this collaboration. The abstract reports an 80% mAP improvement over the best-performing alternative, a relative improvement rather than an increase of 80 percentage points.
neurips-2023-coda-collaborative-novel-bo.tldr: CoDA jointly discovers novel 3D object boxes and aligns point-cloud, image, and text features to improve open-vocabulary detection.

paragraphs: Invariant graph learning seeks patterns that remain useful when the environment changes. Because labels identifying graph environments are expensive to obtain, methods often create additional environment information through augmentation. This paper examines whether that generated information is actually sufficient to reveal stable graph structure.

The authors establish that environment augmentation alone cannot identify invariant graph representations without additional assumptions. They introduce minimal assumptions that include variation sufficiency and variation consistency. Their framework, GALA, then uses an assistant model that is deliberately sensitive to environmental changes. Whether its proxy predictions are correct helps distinguish changes in spurious subgraphs.

GALA extracts a subgraph that is maximally invariant to those proxy predictions. Under the stated assumptions, the authors prove that this procedure identifies the underlying invariant subgraph, supporting out-of-distribution generalization. Experiments across graph distribution shifts, including DrugOOD, demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution connects a practical learning strategy to explicit conditions under which augmented information can reveal invariance.
neurips-2023-does-invariant-graph-learni.tldr: GALA uses an environment-sensitive assistant to identify invariant graph structure under explicit assumptions that environment augmentation alone cannot replace.

paragraphs: Shortcut learning can occur even when a stable feature already determines the label and a shortcut adds no information in the training distribution. This paper investigates why standard training still favors the shortcut in that situation. Its focus is gradient descent applied to log-loss, a combination the authors call default-ERM.

Through a linear perception task, the authors show that this training procedure's preference for maximum-margin solutions can make predictions depend more on the shortcut than on the stable feature. This happens even without overparameterization. The result identifies the optimization procedure's implicit preference as a source of shortcut reliance, beyond explanations based solely on differences between training and deployment data.

The authors instead study uniform margins. In their linear task, uniform margins guarantee dependence only on the perfect stable feature. They propose margin-control losses that encourage such solutions and report reduced shortcut learning across vision and language tasks. The guarantee belongs to the analyzed linear setting; the broader task results provide empirical support for changing the training bias.
neurips-2023-dont-blame-dataset-shift-sh.tldr: Standard gradient-based log-loss training can favor redundant shortcuts, while losses encouraging uniform margins reduce shortcut reliance.

paragraphs: Object-recognition networks often rely heavily on texture, whereas human vision tends to emphasize shape and structure. This paper tests whether sparse coding, a principle associated with the brain, can help produce a stronger preference for shape in neural networks. The intervention concerns which activations remain active inside the network.

The authors enforce sparsity through a nondifferentiable Top-K operation. They report that this constraint can cause convolutional-network neurons to encode structure, with objects represented through parts and smaller subparts. The resulting shape bias emerges from the sparse coding constraint itself, linking the form of internal representations to the visual properties the network emphasizes.

Experiments across network structures and datasets show different functional benefits. Recognition networks become more robust to distracting style and pattern changes, while generative adversarial networks produce images with more coherent, decomposable structures. Ablations suggest that sparse representations tend to favor structure and more distributed representations tend to favor texture. These findings support activation sparsity as a useful design choice for encouraging shape-sensitive visual processing.
neurips-2023-emergence-of-shape-bias-in-.tldr: Enforcing sparse activations can encourage convolutional networks to represent shapes and parts, improving robustness and generated-image structure in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Random-feature methods learn using a collection of randomly constructed features. This paper analyzes their prediction error when outputs are vector-valued, developing theory for ridge regression in a setting that allows both inputs and outputs to be infinite-dimensional. The results also apply to finite-dimensional problems and improve existing analyses there.

The main methodological change is to analyze the prediction-risk functional directly. Comparable approaches work through an explicit solution formula involving random matrices. Avoiding that formula removes the need for concentration results from random matrix theory or extensions to random operators, giving a different route to understanding how learning error behaves.

The authors establish strong consistency even when the model is misspecified. When the model is well specified, they obtain minimax-optimal convergence rates, matching the best worst-case rates for the setting. They also characterize the numbers of random features and labeled examples needed to achieve those rates. These complexity requirements follow Monte Carlo-style scaling and contain no logarithmic factors.
neurips-2023-error-bounds-for-learning-w.tldr: A direct risk analysis establishes consistency and optimal convergence guarantees for vector-valued random-feature ridge regression without random-matrix concentration arguments.

paragraphs: GPT4Tools aims to give open-source language models the ability to operate multimodal tools. The motivation is that sophisticated tool use has been demonstrated with proprietary models whose computational demands and inaccessible data make them difficult to reproduce. The paper develops a training approach for models such as LLaMA and OPT.

An advanced teacher model receives varied multimodal contexts and generates an instruction-following dataset. The authors use this generated supervision to adapt the target models with Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA. The resulting tool-use abilities allow the language models to address visual tasks, including understanding images and generating them through the available tools.

The paper also introduces a benchmark for evaluating tool use in zero-shot and fine-tuned settings. Experiments across several language models report improved accuracy when invoking tools encountered during training, together with zero-shot capability for previously unseen tools. The findings support teacher-generated instruction data as a way to transfer tool-use behavior and extend it beyond the tools directly represented during training.
neurips-2023-gpt4tools-teaching-large-la.tldr: GPT4Tools trains open-source language models on teacher-generated instructions to improve multimodal tool use, including zero-shot use of unseen tools.

paragraphs: Single-index models depend on one projection of their input, so learning them involves finding an informative direction. Earlier analyses for isotropic data connect the required number of samples to an information exponent. This paper studies what changes when the input covariance has a spike, meaning that variation is stronger along a particular direction.

The authors show that commonly used spherical gradient dynamics can fail to recover the target direction in this structured setting, even when the covariance spike points exactly toward it. They then show that an appropriate weight normalization, reminiscent of batch normalization, can alleviate the problem. Helpful input structure therefore does not automatically make every gradient-based procedure successful.

With suitable normalization and alignment between the covariance structure and the target, the analysis yields better sample complexity than in the isotropic case. For a sufficiently large spike, the sample requirement can become independent of the information exponent. In that regime, gradient-based training also beats lower bounds applying to rotationally invariant kernel methods.
neurips-2023-gradient-based-feature-lear.tldr: Appropriate normalization lets gradient-based learning exploit aligned covariance structure, improving sample complexity under a sufficiently strong spike.

paragraphs: A common model-selection strategy assumes that better performance on familiar data predicts better performance after a distribution shift. This paper examines when that assumption breaks down. It shows inverse relationships between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance across multiple real-world datasets, extending the issue beyond constructed worst-case examples.

The authors provide a theoretical explanation for how these inverse relationships arise. They also argue that earlier studies missed them because their methods examined biased selections of models. Which models enter a comparison can therefore change the apparent relationship between performance on familiar data and performance under a shift.

The implication is conditional but consequential: in some settings, improving shifted-data performance requires giving up some familiar-data performance. Continued optimization of the latter can yield diminishing and eventually negative returns for the former. In those cases, selecting models only by in-distribution performance necessarily excludes the best out-of-distribution choices. The findings challenge the reliability of that selection rule without claiming that the relationship is always negative.
neurips-2023-id-and-ood-performance-are-.tldr: Real-world datasets can exhibit inverse ID–OOD performance relationships, making selection by ID performance alone miss the best OOD models.

paragraphs: This paper studies how language-model behavior changes when a prompt asks the model to adopt a persona. The personas describe either social identities or areas of expertise and appear before the task instructions. The researchers use these prompts to investigate role-dependent behavior across language tasks and tasks involving visual information.

In a multi-armed bandit task, models prompted to act as children of different ages display exploration patterns resembling human developmental stages. In language-based reasoning, relevant expert personas outperform personas without the corresponding expertise. In category description, asking for a bird expert produces better bird descriptions than asking for a car expert.

Persona effects also expose bias. A model prompted to act as a man describes cars better than one prompted to act as a woman. This is a finding about the model's response to identity cues, not evidence about people's abilities. Together, the experiments show that in-context impersonation can both improve task performance and reveal hidden associations that influence a model's output.
neurips-2023-in-context-impersonation-re.tldr: Persona prompts change language-model behavior, sometimes improving task performance while also revealing expertise-related and social biases.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix from linear measurements means reconstructing its entries from weighted sums. Here, each measurement is corrupted by independent Gaussian noise, and success means achieving a small relative squared reconstruction error. Near the noise level where recovery remains possible, known non-adaptive methods require measurements on the scale of the matrix's total number of entries.

The paper asks whether choosing later measurements based on earlier responses can avoid that burden. It proves a lower bound on the number of adaptive rounds: an algorithm taking k measurements per round and succeeding with probability at least 9/10 needs Ω(log(n²/k) / log log n) rounds for an n-by-n matrix in the studied setting.

Consequently, using n^(2−β) measurements per round, for any fixed positive β, requires Ω(log n / log log n) rounds. This establishes a trade-off between measurements per round and sequential interaction. The techniques also extend to tensor recovery and related numerical linear algebra tasks, including low-rank and singular-vector approximation.
neurips-2023-lower-bounds-on-adaptive-se.tldr: Lower bounds show that reducing measurements per round in adaptive matrix recovery requires sufficiently many sequential rounds.

paragraphs: A neutral text query can still return image results with unequal gender or racial representation. This paper studies how to reduce that imbalance while keeping search results useful. Its fairness objective concerns equal representation in the retrieved results, even when the query itself contains no explicit demographic connotations.

Earlier approaches try to remove gender and race information from the image and text representations learned by a vision-language model. The authors show that this can be insufficient because the image collection being searched may itself contain test-time bias. They introduce Post-hoc Bias Mitigation, or PBM, which adjusts the outputs of an already trained vision-language model.

Evaluation uses the Occupation 1 and 2 image-search datasets and the MS-COCO and Flickr30k image-text datasets. PBM achieves the lowest reported bias among the compared mitigation methods while maintaining satisfactory retrieval performance. The findings highlight the target retrieval collection as an important source of unequal representation and support output-level adjustment as a practical way to address it.
neurips-2023-mitigating-test-time-bias-f.tldr: PBM post-processes vision-language search outputs to reduce demographic imbalance caused by test-time retrieval data while maintaining satisfactory search performance.

paragraphs: Multimodal training can use natural documents containing images interspersed with text, rather than only isolated image-text pairs. The abstract describes benchmark advantages for models trained on such documents, but notes that the underlying datasets and collection procedures have often been unavailable. OBELICS addresses this access and documentation gap.

The dataset contains 141 million web pages drawn from Common Crawl, with 353 million associated images and 115 billion text tokens. The authors explain how they created it, provide detailed filtering rules, and analyze its contents. These contributions make both the training material and its construction process available for examination and reuse.

To demonstrate that the dataset supports multimodal learning, the authors train models with 9 billion and 80 billion parameters, called IDEFICS-9B and IDEFICS. They report competitive results across different multimodal benchmarks. Releasing the dataset, models, and code provides a shared basis for work on learning from interleaved documents, with trained models serving as evidence of the dataset's practical viability.
neurips-2023-obelics-an-open-web-scale-f.tldr: OBELICS releases a large, documented collection of interleaved image-text web documents and demonstrates its usefulness through competitive multimodal models.

paragraphs: Clustering a finite sample is useful only insofar as the resulting groups represent the underlying population. This paper studies how quickly a clustering solution learned from n independent samples approaches the optimal clustering for a fixed, unknown distribution. It covers both ordinary point centers and centers represented by low-dimensional subspaces.

For point-centered objectives, the authors obtain a convergence rate of approximately sqrt(k/n), up to logarithmic factors, where k is the number of clusters. This matches known optimal results for k-means and extends the rate to objectives such as k-median. For clustering around j-dimensional subspaces, they derive an upper rate of approximately sqrt(kj²/n), again up to logarithmic factors.

The authors also prove a lower bound of order sqrt(kj/n) for projective clustering. This identifies an unavoidable dependence on the number and dimension of the subspaces and supports the essential optimality of earlier bounds. Together, the results quantify how sample requirements grow as the clustering representation becomes more complex.
neurips-2023-on-generalization-bounds-fo.tldr: New generalization bounds quantify how clustering accuracy depends on sample size, cluster count, and subspace dimension.

paragraphs: A matrix can have several simplifying structures at once: only a few rows may be nonzero, while its rows and columns also obey a low-rank structure. This paper studies recovery of such matrices from linear observations. The aim is to exploit both forms of structure together when measurements are limited.

The proposed method uses iteratively reweighted least squares, repeatedly solving weighted fitting problems. Its objective combines nonconvex approximations to row sparsity and rank, with a balancing mechanism built into the algorithm. This joint treatment is intended to use the information supplied by both structures rather than relying on just one.

The authors prove locally quadratic convergence in a regime with nearly minimal sample complexity, allowing constants and a logarithmic factor. The local qualification matters: the result describes convergence near the structured solution. The abstract states that combining convex surrogates cannot achieve this sample regime. Experiments also show favorable convergence and recovery from fewer measurements than the state-of-the-art methods compared.
neurips-2023-recovering-simultaneously-s.tldr: A nonconvex reweighted least-squares method jointly exploits row sparsity and low rank, with local quadratic convergence at nearly minimal sample complexity.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents often observe only part of the situation they must act on, making memory necessary for interpreting current observations. Many methods summarize experience using memory architectures borrowed from supervised learning. This paper argues that reinforcement learning's different training and efficiency characteristics motivate a memory model designed specifically for it.

Fast and Forgetful Memory constrains the possible memory mechanisms using strong structural assumptions inspired by computational psychology. It is designed to work across learning algorithms and to replace recurrent neural networks inside recurrent reinforcement-learning systems. This makes it possible to examine the effect of the memory component while retaining the surrounding learning procedure.

Across the reported recurrent benchmarks and algorithms, the replacement achieves higher reward without changing hyperparameters. The authors also report training speeds two orders of magnitude faster than recurrent neural networks, attributing the advantage to logarithmic time and linear space complexity. The results support specialized memory structure as a way to improve both learning performance and computational efficiency in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2023-reinforcement-learning-with.tldr: Fast and Forgetful Memory replaces recurrent networks in reinforcement learning, achieving higher rewards and substantially faster training in the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: Machine-learning systems may need to satisfy fairness, robustness, or safety requirements alongside predictive accuracy. Choosing the strength of those requirements is difficult because their effects and trade-offs may become clear only during training. Resilient constrained learning addresses this problem by adapting requirements while solving the learning task.

The approach allows constraints to be relaxed, but assigns a user-defined cost to that relaxation. Training balances the performance gained by loosening a requirement against the cost of doing so. This makes the compromise part of the learning problem itself, with the user's cost specification expressing how much relaxation is acceptable relative to task improvement.

The paper gives conditions under which this balance can be achieved and presents a practical algorithm with approximation and generalization guarantees. Applications include image classification with multiple possible invariances and federated learning under distribution shift. These examples demonstrate the advantages of adapting constraints when their interaction with the task is difficult to assess in advance.
neurips-2023-resilient-constrained-learn.tldr: Resilient constrained learning adapts training requirements by balancing the performance benefits of relaxation against user-defined costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies how attention patterns emerge during next-token training in a transformer with one self-attention layer and one decoder layer. It analyzes stochastic gradient descent directly, asking how a simple predictive objective leads the model to combine input tokens in a particular way.

The proof assumes no positional encoding, long input sequences, and a decoder that learns faster than the attention layer. Under these conditions, initially uniform attention becomes a discriminative scanning process. It emphasizes key tokens that distinguish a particular predicted next token and downweights tokens shared across different predictions. Among distinctive tokens, attention is progressively dropped in order from lower to higher key-query co-occurrence in the training data.

This pruning does not continue to a single winning token. A phase transition, controlled by the decoder's learning rate, stops the process and leaves an almost fixed combination of tokens. The authors verify this scan-and-snap pattern on synthetic data and WikiText-103, connecting a conditional mathematical account of training to observed representation formation.
neurips-2023-scan-and-snap-understanding.tldr: Under explicit assumptions, a one-layer transformer's attention scans for discriminative tokens before a learning-rate-dependent transition fixes their combination.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo produces samples used to approximate a target probability distribution. Stein-based post-processing can improve an existing chain's output by assigning weights to its visited states. This paper asks how to design the chain itself when that later weighting step is part of the plan.

The method lets the chain have an invariant distribution Π while its weighted output approximates the desired target P. The authors show that the optimal Π for this purpose differs from P. They use a new variational argument to construct Π explicitly, thereby coordinating sample generation with the post-processing procedure rather than choosing them independently.

The paper establishes explicit conditions for convergence of the resulting Stein Π-Importance Sampling method. On approximately 70% of tasks in the PosteriorDB benchmark, it reports significant improvements over analogous post-processing of chains whose invariant distribution is P. The result supports designing the sampling distribution around the final weighted approximation, while the benchmark claim concerns a majority of tested tasks rather than every task.
neurips-2023-stein-pi-importance-samplin.tldr: Designing a Markov chain for Stein reweighting can favor an invariant distribution different from the target and improve the final approximation.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning requires more than recognizing the contents of an image. A model must also identify relationships and reuse abstract patterns on unfamiliar inputs. This paper addresses a gap between models that extract individual objects from complex scenes and models that generalize relational rules but assume object-focused inputs are already available.

Object-Centric Relational Abstraction, or OCRA, combines these capabilities. It extracts explicit representations of objects and abstract relations from visual input. Bringing the two together gives the reasoning process both identifiable entities and a representation of how those entities relate, connecting scene interpretation with the abstractions needed for systematic generalization.

The authors report strong systematic generalization on tasks involving complex visual displays. Their evaluation includes CLEVR-ART, a new dataset with greater visual complexity. The findings support combining object-centered perception with relational abstraction when learned patterns must transfer to novel inputs. The contribution is the integrated model and its demonstrated generalization on these tasks, motivated by the complementary strengths of the two earlier approaches.
neurips-2023-systematic-visual-reasoning.tldr: OCRA combines explicit object representations with relational abstraction to generalize visual patterns across complex, unfamiliar inputs.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often pool information by replacing a graph with a smaller, coarser representation. This creates local summaries of both graph structure and vertex features. The paper asks whether that compression preserves the distinctions already captured by preceding message-passing layers, an issue less studied than the expressiveness of message passing itself.

The authors derive sufficient conditions under which a pooling operator fully preserves that preceding expressive power. These conditions provide a theoretical criterion for choosing existing pooling methods and designing new ones. Because the conditions are sufficient, satisfying them establishes preservation; failing them alone does not establish that an operator must always lose expressive power.

The paper uses the criterion to examine existing operators and identify those that do not satisfy it. It also introduces an experimental setup based on graph-isomorphism testing to assess the distinguishing ability of networks with pooling layers. Together, the theory and evaluation setup make information preservation an explicit consideration when comparing methods for compressing graph representations.
neurips-2023-the-expressive-power-of-poo.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions for graph pooling to preserve preceding message-passing expressiveness and a setup for testing that ability.

paragraphs: Confidence intervals and p-values describe uncertainty arising from observing a sample instead of a whole population. A separate problem arises when the population itself changes across places or times. This paper introduces the s-value to assess how sensitive a statistical parameter is to such distributional changes.

The proposed measure evaluates instability within a neighborhood defined by Kullback-Leibler divergence, which specifies the allowed size of a distributional perturbation. The authors also consider shifts restricted to particular directions or variables. These more targeted assessments help identify which kinds of changes could reverse a statistical conclusion, making the source of instability more interpretable.

The paper discusses how this information can guide data collection when transferring estimates between distributions. Evaluations on real data show that the measure can reveal sensitivity to particular shifts and can help improve estimation accuracy under changed distributions. Its contribution is to make distributional stability an explicit object of analysis alongside sampling uncertainty, connecting that diagnosis to decisions about obtaining more informative data.
neurips-2023-the-s-value-evaluating-stab.tldr: The s-value measures a statistical parameter's sensitivity to distribution shifts and can guide data collection and estimation under changed conditions.

paragraphs: During gradient descent, loss sharpness can initially rise and then settle near twice the reciprocal of the step size. Sharpness here means the largest eigenvalue of the loss Hessian, a measure of local curvature. This paper investigates the training dynamics behind that progressive sharpening and eventual edge-of-stability behavior.

The authors first observe empirically that, when edge-of-stability behavior occurs, trajectories from different initializations align after a suitable reparameterization. They fall on a shared bifurcation diagram, giving a common description of paths that initially appear different. This alignment offers a way to relate the evolving curvature to the broader dynamics of training.

The paper then rigorously proves trajectory alignment for a two-layer fully connected linear network and a single-neuron nonlinear network trained with one data point. Within those analyzed settings, the alignment framework establishes both progressive sharpening and edge-of-stability behavior. The contribution combines a broader empirical observation with proofs for specific simplified networks, extending earlier explanations through a common dynamical picture.
neurips-2023-trajectory-alignment-unders.tldr: Aligned gradient-descent trajectories provide a bifurcation-based explanation of progressive sharpening and edge-of-stability behavior, with proofs for specific simple networks.

paragraphs: Lidar can record when photons return from a scene, producing time-resolved histograms richer than a derived point cloud. Earlier lidar-supervised neural radiance fields mainly used point clouds to help render ordinary camera images. This paper instead models the raw measurements from a single-photon lidar and predicts them from new viewpoints.

The method uses a time-resolved volume-rendering equation to represent how light travels through the scene. This lets the model capture transient effects at picosecond timescales and synthesize photon-count histograms. The authors evaluate it using simulated scans and captured multiview measurements from a prototype single-photon lidar.

The results demonstrate novel-view rendering of transient imagery. When training from few viewpoints, the approach also recovers better geometry and conventional appearance than point-cloud-based supervision. These findings show the value of incorporating the lidar measurement process directly into scene learning. The authors identify simulation of raw lidar signals for autonomous driving, robotics, and remote sensing as possible applications of the approach.
neurips-2023-transient-neural-radiance-f.tldr: Transient NeRFs learn from raw photon-arrival histograms to render lidar measurements from new views and improve reconstruction with few input viewpoints.
